CO adsorbed and desorbed from the three-filter configuration during bench cycling 2 The adsorption/desorption performance over 70 cycles is shown in Figure 17. The results show a noticeable decline in working capacity. It was suspected that hot spots may have formed throughout the filter surface. To verify this, a filter was removed and heated to 80 °C. The temperature distribution was analyzed with a thermal imaging camera, which exposed several hot spots on the filter, particularly within the pleat fold (Figure 18). In addition to sorbent degradation at high temperatures, migration of the filter adhesive during the process that could occlude capture sites or pores in the sorbent surface may also have contributed to the observed degradation. DE-FE0032254 An alternative layered/laminate filter design was evaluated to address the limitations of the pleated filter design. Layering flat filters offers thermal insulation during the desorption period, electrical insulation between heating layers, and thermal mass in the axial direction to absorb minor heating nonuniformities due to various defects that can occur in the manufacturing of the electrically conductive substrate or in the sorbent coating process. To test this approach, five flat sorbent coated filters were assembled in the bench unit for testing. The ends of five flat filter sheets were coated with conductive paint, and a copper mesh electrode was installed along the ends for electrical continuity. Thermocouples were placed between the central layers for temperature measurement and feedback control. Cycle
